sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Throughput is the number of requests, operations, or bytes a system successfully processes per unit of time — measured in requests/sec (req/s), messages/sec (msg/s), or megabytes/sec (MB/s) — and represents the *aggregate capacity* of a system rather than any single user's experience.

Throughput is the answer to "how much work can this system do in parallel?" Where latency measures the experience of *one* request, throughput measures how many requests can be in flight simultaneously before the system saturates. The two are not independent: they are tied together by **Little's Law**, which states that in a stable system `L = λ · W`, where `L` is the average number of requests in the system, `λ` is arrival rate (throughput), and `W` is the average time each request spends in the system (latency). Rearranged as `λ = L / W`, this becomes the single most useful equation in capacity planning: throughput equals the number of concurrent in-flight requests divided by the per-request latency. If your service has 100 worker threads and each request takes 50 ms, the theoretical ceiling is `100 / 0.050 = 2,000 req/s`. Push beyond that and queues grow without bound.

Why does throughput matter in real systems? Because business load is measured in volume, not in single requests. Netflix serves tens of millions of concurrent streams; Amazon's Prime Day drives hundreds of thousands of checkout transactions per minute; Uber dispatches millions of trip requests per hour. Each backend service must be sized so that *aggregate* throughput exceeds peak arrival rate with headroom — usually 30–50% above forecast peak. If throughput falls below arrival rate, queues fill, latency explodes, and the system enters a death spiral where slow requests hold resources that block newer requests.

The canonical real-world example is **Kafka at LinkedIn**, which by 2019 was processing roughly **7 trillion messages per day** across thousands of brokers. LinkedIn's published numbers cite sustained throughput in the hundreds of millions of messages per second cluster-wide, with single brokers pushing several hundred thousand messages/sec on commodity hardware. The two levers Kafka pulls to reach those numbers are **batching** and **sequential I/O**. Producers batch many records into a single produce request; brokers append batches sequentially to an OS page cache-backed log; consumers read sequentially. Switching from one-record-per-request to 1,000-records-per-request typically improves Kafka throughput by an order of magnitude — batching amortizes per-request overhead (network round-trip, RPC framing, fsync, replica fetch) across many records.

Throughput bottlenecks are usually one of four things: CPU saturation, disk IOPS / bandwidth, network bandwidth, or lock contention. Profiling a system to find the bottleneck is critical because optimizing the wrong dimension produces nothing. A CPU-bound service will not improve by adding more network bandwidth; a network-bound service will not improve by adding more CPU. The **Universal Scalability Law** (Gunther) extends Amdahl's law by adding a *coherence penalty* term: as concurrency rises, cross-thread coordination (locks, cache invalidation, consensus rounds) eats into throughput gains, so real systems show a *concave* throughput curve that eventually *declines* past some concurrency level. This is why adding threads to a contended database can reduce throughput.

The classic pitfall is **confusing throughput with latency**. A common anti-pattern is "we measured 10,000 req/s in load testing, so we're fine" — but if those 10,000 req/s come at p99 = 5 seconds, real users will abandon. The correct SLO is a *joint* throughput-latency bound: "the system must sustain ≥5,000 req/s with p99 latency ≤ 200 ms." Without the latency bound, throughput numbers are meaningless because they can be achieved by queueing everything. Conversely, optimizing latency at the cost of throughput (e.g., tiny batches, no pipelining) leaves the system unable to handle peak load.

A second real-world illustration is **Redis pipelining**, which mirrors Kafka's batching insight at the in-memory tier. Without pipelining, a single Redis `SET` per network round-trip on a 1 ms RTT link tops out at ~1,000 ops/sec per connection — the network round-trip, not Redis, is the bottleneck. With pipelining (sending 100 commands in a single round-trip), the same connection sustains ~100,000 ops/sec, a 100× gain. Instagram's feed service uses Redis pipelining extensively to push hundreds of thousands of cache updates per second on a small fleet. The pattern repeats everywhere: gRPC multiplexing, HTTP/2 frame batching, database `INSERT ... VALUES (...), (...), ...` multi-row statements, and CPU instruction pipelining all exploit the same principle — amortize the per-request fixed cost across many units of work.

Throughput also drives the **economics** of a system. Cloud bills are denominated in vCPU-hours and GB-hours, and the throughput-per-dollar ratio determines whether your unit economics work. A service that processes 10,000 req/s on a $5/hr instance has a unit cost of $0.0005 per million requests; the same service at 1,000 req/s costs $0.005 per million — ten times more expensive per unit of value. This is why every performance engineering effort eventually becomes a cost-engineering effort: raising throughput per instance directly lowers cost per request. Amazon's retail services obsess over this metric because at their scale, a 10% throughput improvement per instance translates to millions of dollars in annual infrastructure savings.

Throughput connects to nearly every other system design concept. It trades off against **latency** (larger batches → higher throughput but higher per-item latency). It is bounded by **availability** and **fault tolerance** (a failed replica reduces effective throughput). It is multiplied by **scalability** (horizontal scaling multiplies throughput linearly if coherence penalty is low). It is constrained by **consistency models** (synchronous replication cuts throughput; Cassandra's quorum writes are slower but more consistent than `ONE` writes). And it is the primary input to **capacity planning** — the exercise of mapping forecast business load to provisioned hardware.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Producer Pool] -->|batch of N records| B[Broker Leader]
    B -->|sequential append| C[(OS Page Cache / Disk Log)]
    B -->|fetch batches| D[Replica Follower 1]
    B -->|fetch batches| E[Replica Follower 2]
    C -->|sequential read| F[Consumer Group]
    F --> G[Throughput = records / sec]

    H[Little's Law] --> I[Throughput = Concurrency / Latency]
    I --> G

    style G fill:#cfc,stroke:#060
    style I fill:#fcc,stroke:#600
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
                 Throughput ceiling = Concurrency / Latency
   +------------------------------------------------------------+
   |                                                            |
   |   Producer --batch(1000)--> Broker --append--> Log on disk |
   |      |                         |                           |
   |      |                         |--replicate--> Follower A  |
   |      |                         +--replicate--> Follower B  |
   |      |                                                     |
   |      +-- Little's Law:  lambda = L / W                     |
   |           lambda = throughput                              |
   |           L = concurrent in-flight requests                |
   |           W = per-request latency                          |
   |                                                            |
   +------------------------------------------------------------+

   Throughput vs concurrency curve (Universal Scalability Law):
   TPS
    ^
    |         .---^---.       <- peak throughput
    |       /         \
    |     /             \     <- coherence penalty (locks)
    |   /                 \
    | /                     \
    +--------------------------> concurrency
```

### Walkthrough
1. Producers accumulate records into batches of N (e.g., 1,000 records or 16 KB) to amortize per-request overhead. Without batching, each record pays a full network round-trip and broker append cost.
2. The broker leader appends each batch sequentially to an OS-page-cache-backed log. Sequential disk writes on modern NVMe sustain gigabytes per second, far above what random I/O could achieve.
3. Followers fetch batches in pipeline, replicating to in-sync replicas. Consumers read sequentially from the log. Throughput is reported as records/sec sustained cluster-wide — bounded by Little's Law: concurrency (in-flight batches) divided by end-to-end latency per batch.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
Little's Law throughput simulator.
throughput = concurrency / latency
Demonstrates how batching, concurrency, and latency trade off.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List

@dataclass
class SystemConfig:
    name: str
    workers: int          # concurrent in-flight requests (L in Little's Law)
    latency_ms: float     # per-request latency (W)
    batch_size: int       # records per request

@dataclass
class ThroughputResult:
    name: str
    req_per_sec: float
    records_per_sec: float
    theoretical_ceiling: float

def little_law_throughput(workers: int, latency_ms: float) -> float:
    """Little's Law: lambda = L / W.  Returns req/sec."""
    return workers / (latency_ms / 1000.0)

def simulate(config: SystemConfig) -> ThroughputResult:
    rps = little_law_throughput(config.workers, config.latency_ms)
    recs = rps * config.batch_size
    return ThroughputResult(
        name=config.name,
        req_per_sec=round(rps, 1),
        records_per_sec=round(recs, 1),
        theoretical_ceiling=round(rps, 1),
    )

def usl_throughput(n_workers: int, alpha: float, beta: float, sigma: float) -> float:
    """
    Universal Scalability Law:  X(N) = (alpha * N) / (1 + beta*(N-1) + sigma*N*(N-1))
    - alpha: throughput of a single worker
    - beta:  contention penalty (locking)
    - sigma: coherence penalty (cache invalidation, cross-talk)
    Demonstrates that adding workers eventually STOPS helping and can HURT.
    """
    if n_workers <= 0:
        return 0.0
    n = n_workers
    denom = 1 + beta * (n - 1) + sigma * n * (n - 1)
    return (alpha * n) / denom

if __name__ == "__main__":
    configs = [
        SystemConfig("no-batch-50-threads",   workers=50,  latency_ms=20,  batch_size=1),
        SystemConfig("batch-50-threads",      workers=50,  latency_ms=20,  batch_size=1000),
        SystemConfig("no-batch-500-threads",  workers=500, latency_ms=20,  batch_size=1),
        SystemConfig("batch-500-threads",     workers=500, latency_ms=20,  batch_size=1000),
    ]

    print(f"{'Config':<28} {'req/s':>10} {'rec/s':>14}")
    print("-" * 56)
    for c in configs:
        r = simulate(c)
        print(f"{r.name:<28} {r.req_per_sec:>10} {r.records_per_sec:>14}")

    print("\nUniversal Scalability Law: peak concurrency vs throughput")
    print(f"{'workers':>8} {'throughput':>12}")
    print("-" * 22)
    for n in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512]:
        t = usl_throughput(n, alpha=100, beta=0.01, sigma=0.0005)
        print(f"{n:>8} {t:>12.1f}")
    print("\nNote: throughput rises, peaks, then FALLS due to coherence penalty.")
```
